Chapter 6: The Practice of Presence—Finding Christ in the Everyday.
You know, there’s a gentle wisdom that comes from just noticing the world as it really is, not as we wish it to be. For a lot of us, Christ’s teachings can feel pretty distant—like they only belong in church or during special moments. But honestly, there’s an invitation waiting for us in the quiet, everyday spaces of life. It’s an invitation to discover something sacred right where we already are.
Picture this: a woman, exhausted from her busy job and the never-ending list of chores, stands at her kitchen window. The sun’s rising, painting everything gold—even the sink full of dishes. She pauses, takes a breath, and just stands there in the stillness. In that ordinary moment, she feels a sense of peace. It’s this gentle reminder that the sacred isn’t far away at all—it’s woven into the fabric of our daily lives.
That’s really the heart of the practice of presence. In many Asian traditions, mindfulness isn’t just a technique—it’s a whole way of being. It’s about showing up fully, whether life feels joyful or hard, ordinary or extraordinary. Christ’s own teachings echo this. He noticed the lilies in the field, the sparrows in the sky, the needs of people around him. He was truly alive in every moment, meeting people right where they were.
Most of us rush through our days, stuck on worries about the future or regrets from the past. But what if you could slow down, pay attention, and actually find Christ in the here and now? He’s there in the laughter of a child, the taste of a simple meal, or the quiet hush of early morning. Presence isn’t about escaping reality; it’s about stepping into it even more deeply.
There’s another story—a young man dealing with anxiety who starts a simple daily habit: he sits quietly for a few minutes and just notices his breath. At first, it feels awkward. But as days go by, those quiet moments help him face the day with more clarity and compassion. He starts to notice small joys—a bird singing outside, sunlight warming his face. The world doesn’t really change, but his way of being in it does.
Practicing presence isn’t about getting it perfect. It’s about coming back, again and again, to this moment right now. When your mind drifts, as it always will, just come back—notice, breathe, and be. The ordinary becomes extraordinary. The everyday becomes holy.
Christ’s presence wasn’t just found in grand miracles or big dramatic moments. You see it in the way he listened deeply, the way he touched the sick, the way he shared meals—whether with friends or strangers. His life is proof of how powerful it is to be fully present—to God, to others, to the world around us.
In Eastern traditions, presence is often practiced through simple rituals—maybe lighting incense, bowing, chanting, or just sitting in silence. These aren’t about the ritual itself, but about opening a door to deeper awareness. They remind us that every moment is a chance to encounter something divine.
There’s a father, overwhelmed by the chaos of family life, who tries something small: he lights a candle at dinner each night. This simple act becomes a signal—pause, breathe, be together. Over time, family meals shift. They become moments of connection, gratitude, and presence.
The beautiful thing is, the practice of presence is open to everyone—no special knowledge or spiritual status required. All it really asks is your attention—a willingness to show up, to notice, and to receive the gift of each moment.
In a world that’s always pushing us to go faster, do more, this way of living can seem almost radical. But it leads to peace, to joy, and to a deeper sense of Christ’s presence right in the midst of daily life.
